reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked for orange paint. There was no orange paint at all.

"What can I do?" Norah asked her teacher. Her teacher smiled. "Ask Milo. He knows a trick."

Milo came over with two pots. He dipped his brush in red paint. Then he dipped it in yellow paint. He stirred them together on his paper. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned orange! It smelled a little stinky, like all the paints did.

Norah dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred. Orange! She painted her pumpkin round and bright.

"I did it," said Norah. "Red and yellow make orange."

Milo laughed. "Now pay me back with a big smile."

Norah smiled her biggest smile. Then she painted a green leaf on top.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. The hairdresser, Mia, snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down like snow.

Beatrice looked in the wall mirror. She could see the front of her hair. It was short now. "I want to see the back," said Beatrice. She turned her head. She could not see the back. She stuck out her chin. She turned again. Still no back. "I can't see it," she said. "That is not bad," said Mia. "I have an idea."

Mia held up a little mirror in her hand. She held it behind Beatrice. Beatrice looked at the wall mirror. There it was! The back of her hair. She could see it in the small mirror. "I see it! I see the back!" said Beatrice. She wiggled her toes. "Do it again," she said. Mia smiled and held the little mirror up once more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Brooklyn got her red coat from her room. But the coat was not on the hook. It was on the floor, under her toy carrot! "Where is my coat?" she asked. She looked and looked. There it was, down low, all crumpled up.

Mama hung the coat on the hook. "Now it waits up high," said Mama. Brooklyn put her arms in the sleeves. One arm, two arms. Then she pulled the zipper. Up, up, up it went. Zzzz! The coat was warm and furry like a cat.

At the bus stop, Brooklyn waited. The bus was not here yet. So she dreamed about the carrot in her pocket. The bus came. She climbed up. "I zipped it all by myself," she said. Mama smiled and zipped her own coat too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table for breakfast. The sky outside was cloudy. "Sniff, sniff," went Victoria's nose.

Mama gave her warm oatmeal. Victoria took a bite. "Sniff, sniff," went her nose again. She wiped it on her sleeve. Her sleeve got wet and sticky. That did not feel good.

"Let's name what your nose needs," said Mama. "A napkin? No. A towel? No. A tissue? Yes!" Victoria took a tissue from the box. She blew her nose, one big toot. Now her nose was clear.

After breakfast, Victoria sat by the window. She could smell her apple now. She watched the big tree sway. "I hope we can play under it soon," she said. She held the tissue box on her lap, all ready.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Elijah put on his skates at the ice rink. The ice looked fresh and shiny. His dad helped him step onto it. His mom held one hand. His friend Nina held the other.

They skated slow. They skated past the snack bar. On a big screen, a basketball game was playing. A man blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. Elijah stood still on his skates. "Why did they stop?" he asked.

Nina pointed at the screen. "The whistle," she said. The whistle blew again. The players started running again. Elijah watched with wide eyes. The whistle blew. The players stopped. The whistle blew. The players ran.

Then the game ended on the screen. Dad bought warm cocoa for everyone. Elijah took a little sip. Mom gave his hair a kiss. They sat and watched the skaters go round and round. Elijah listened for more whistles. "Listen," he said. "That horn means the zamboni is coming."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of many shapes. She found a round block. It rolled away. "Too wobbly!" she said. That block was a circle, and circles roll.

She found a block with three sides. "A triangle!" It made a fine roof, pointy at the top. Then she found a long block with four sides. A rectangle! Perfect for the wall.

She looked for one more square block. Her friend Ben pointed at a tilted block. "Look, a new shape!" he said. "It has a corner pointing up!"

Lillian turned the block back down flat. It was the same square! She laughed. "Silly block. You are still a square!"

She stacked the square at the bottom. The house stood tall. She tucked the snake inside. "Home at last!" said Lillian.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Violet got to daycare in the morning. The sun was low and yellow. She put her coat on her hook. She wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. But paint time was later, after snack.

Violet played with blocks. She poured cold water in the sand table. The sand turned dark and sticky. "Look," said her friend Sam. "The water made it wet."

Violet ate her snack. Then the class went outside. The sun was high now. It was hot on her shoulders. After outside time came lunch. After lunch came a nap.

Violet slept on her little mat. When she woke up, she rubbed her eyes. "Is it morning now?" she asked. "Can I paint now?"

Teacher Mia shook her head and smiled. "It is afternoon now, Violet. The morning went by. It is nap-then-play time."

So it was afternoon. The sun was on the other side of the window. Violet sat at the paint table. She painted a big yellow sun.

"That is for Grandma," she said. Grandma would come this afternoon, after daycare. Tomorrow Violet would paint her a moon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emile wanted to find the dog in the book. He opened the book from the left. The pages went the wrong way. They would not turn.

His friend Noa came over. She held up a small flag with blue stripes. "This book is Hebrew," she said. "It opens from the other side."

Emile looked at the back of the book. He tried it. The cover opened! The thick pages turned one by one.

Noa pointed to the little letters. "We start here," she said. She pointed to the right side of the page. Emile put his finger there too.

They slid their fingers to the left. The letters made words. The words made the story. And there, on the last page, was a big brown dog.

"Woof!" said Emile.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lily loved school. She loved the big blocks and the small cups. She loved the fast slide and the slow snail. The snail left a slimy line on the wall. Lily named her snaily things all morning. "One, the slide. Two, the snail. Three, the blocks."

At nap time, Lily lay on her mat. The teacher turned off the sun lamp. The room went dark. Lily closed her eyes. Then she woke up. The window was black. The stars were out. "It's morning!" Lily began to shout. "I want my snack!"

The teacher came over. She knelt down by the mat. "Look out the window," she said. "It is dark. It is still night. Day and night are opposites." Lily looked. Dark sky, little stars. Not morning at all. Day was bright, and night was dark.

Lily lay back down. The teacher covered her with a soft blanket. The blanket was warm. Lily's water cup was cold. She took one small sip. "One, sip. Two, blanket. Three, sleep," Lily whispered. Then the teacher wrote a letter to Lily's mom. It said Lily slept all night long. Outside, one star blinked, and Lily's eyes blinked too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Raphael was playing house at daycare. He stirred a big pretend soup. His friend Mia held her doll, Baby Nell.

Then Mia dropped Baby Nell on the floor. "Oh no!" she cried. "Baby Nell is hurt!"

The teacher knelt down. "Look," she said softly. "The doll is not hurt. Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Mia wiped her eyes. She picked up Baby Nell. She gave the doll a big pretend hug. "There, there," she said. Baby Nell still looked the same. But now Mia smiled.

Raphael watched. Was that how it worked? He looked at his teddy bear. He squeezed the teddy's paw. The teddy did not say ouch. The teddy was just soft and quiet.

So Raphael tried it too. He held his teddy close. "You lost your sock," he told the teddy. He pulled a thick, cozy sock from the dress-up basket. He put it on the teddy's foot. "Warm now?" he asked.

Mia came over with Baby Nell. "Our babies can play," she said. Raphael gave the teddy another hug. "I thank you for the soup," he said in a small teddy voice.

The teacher brought real juice cups for the children. Raphael drank his juice. The teddy just sat there. That was okay. Pretend hugs were still nice.

Raphael patted the teddy's head. "Nap time," he whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet book. She wanted to know every letter. Mom sat next to her on the soft cushion.

"Let's count them," said Mom. Brielle pointed at each letter. "A, B, C, D." She went on and on. Her sock slipped off one foot, but she kept pointing. "W, X, Y, Z."

"I counted all the way to twenty-six!" said Brielle. Her eyes got big. She counted again to be sure. Twenty-six again!

Then she made the letter sounds. "B says buh. B is for book!" She hugged the book.

"Now let's clean up," said Mom. Brielle put on her sock. She picked up her toys. "A is for away," she said, pushing the truck away from the nook. "A says ah!"

Mom laughed. "You did it, Brielle."

Brielle smiled and traced the letters with her finger, all twenty-six.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Mila wanted to play tea party in her playroom. She set out one big cup and one small cup. The big cup was for Teddy. The small cup was for her. "Pretend tea is not hot," said Mama. "It is cold, like water from the fridge." Mila touched it. "Cold!" she said.

Then Mila found a puddle by the toy shelf. It was small at first. She stepped in it. Splash! Now the puddle was big. Now her socks were wet. "My socks are wet," said Mila. "They were dry before. Wet and dry are opposites, Mama?" Mama smiled. "Yes, wet and dry are opposites." So they got dry socks.

Mila put them on slowly, wiggling her toes. Then she ran fast to the tea table. "Slow toes, fast toes!" she said. Teddy's tail was warm and soft in the sun. Mila hugged him and poured more cold pretend tea.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia filled the big tub. Penelope put her hands in. Splash! The water jumped up. Now her arms were wet.

Splash went Tom next to her. Now his shirt was wet too. Then the water play was over. Tom ran to the blocks. Drip, drip, drip. Water fell on the floor. "Wet boy, wet boy!" laughed Penelope. Tom looked down at his shirt. He was all drippy.

Teacher Mia held up a big soft towel. "Come here, Tom," she said. Tom came back. Mia rubbed the towel on his arms. Rub, rub, rub. The towel drank up all the water. Tom was dry! "My turn," said Penelope. Mia dried her hands too. Then Penelope got the towel and dried her friend Sam, one kind pat at a time. "All dry!" said Penelope. "Now we color." Sam handed her the crayon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Alexander dug three little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed into each one. Then he patted the dirt down with his hands. "Now grow," he said.

Dad filled a small watering can. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. The water made dark wet spots on the soil. "Seeds need water to start growing," said Dad.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. His dog, Biscuit, wagged his tongue and sniffed the ground. "Nothing yet," said Alexander.

He watered the dirt again. He swung the can back and forth. The sun felt warm. A ladybug landed on his new red boot.

The next day, more water. Still just dirt. Alexander waited on the swing and counted clouds.

On the fourth morning, Alexander ran to the garden. Something green was poking up. "A sprout!" he shouted. He knelt down very close. The tiny sprout had two little leaves. Biscuit barked once. Alexander ran to get his watering can.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Mason wanted to hold the red balloon. It was Daddy's balloon from the party.

Mason grabbed for it. The string slipped away. Daddy shook his head. "Try again," Daddy said.

Mason thought hard. He remembered his lion book. The little lion wanted a turn with the ball. The little lion said, "May I have a turn?" Then he got the ball.

Mason took a big breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Daddy smiled wide. "Yes, you may!" Daddy put the string in Mason's hand.

The balloon bumped the ceiling. Mason laughed and laughed. He held the string with both hands. The balloon went up, then down, then up again.

"Thank you, Daddy," Mason said. Daddy gave him a hug. "You asked so nicely," Daddy said. "That was very polite."

Mason walked slowly with the balloon. The lion book sat on the shelf. "Night night, lion," Mason whispered. The balloon floated above his head.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a pencil by his hand. "You can write your name," she said. Jackson picked up the pencil. He held it up high and waved it. Mom took his hand gently. "Point it down," she said. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone." Jackson turned the pencil. The point went down toward the table.

He pressed the pencil to the paper. He made a big round shape. "That is J!" said Mom. Jackson clapped. He tried again. He made an a, then a c. One letter went crooked. It slid off the paper. "I miss one," said Jackson.

"That is okay," said Mom. "Try again." Jackson held the pencil tight. He wrote k, then s, then o, then n. "Jackson!" he shouted. Then the pencil rolled. It stopped by the wet spot near his cup. Jackson picked it up, point down. Mom smiled. "Look at my name!" said Jackson.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Eliana sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Where are we going?" she asked. "To the dentist," said Mom. "She will look at your teeth."

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and up when the dentist pushed a button. Eliana sat in the chair. She opened her mouth wide. Then a bright light above the chair turned on. Eliana squinted. "Too bright!" she said.

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Here, try these," she said. Eliana put them on. Now the light did not hurt her eyes. She could see the light shining right at her mouth. "The light helps me see inside your mouth," said the dentist. She looked at every tooth. "Your teeth are clean and strong," she said.

On the way home, Eliana was hungry. Mom gave her a snack in the car. Eliana chewed slowly. "My teeth taste the apple," she said. "Just like the light saw my teeth?" Mom laughed and drove on. "Can we come back?" Eliana asked. "Next time I want the sunglasses again."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Mohamed wanted a bedtime story. He ran to the shelf and grabbed his book. But it was Dad's old book, the one with funny letters.

Mohamed opened it from the left side. He saw pages with no pictures. He turned one page. Then another. Where were the pictures? He felt dizzy from all the little marks.

"Maybe I opened it the wrong way," he said. He closed the book. Then he opened it from the other side. The first page had a big sun! Under the sun were little marks too.

Dad sat down beside him. "Read with me," said Dad. Dad put his finger at the right side of the page. His finger moved to the left. The marks made words, and the words made the story of a turtle who wanted to grow big.

"Again," said Mohamed. Dad turned the page. His finger started at the right again. Mohamed put his little finger next to Dad's big finger. "My turn," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. He found only three pots. "Red," said Leon. "Yellow. Blue." Three pots. Only three. Leon felt sorry for his rainbow.

Then Leon had a big want. He wanted orange for his rainbow. He dipped his brush in red. He tapped it on the paper. He dipped his brush in yellow. He tapped it next to the red. The red and the yellow sank together. The paint turned orange! Leon clapped his hands.

"Orange, orange, orange!" he sang. He painted a big orange stripe. He dipped in yellow. He dipped in blue. Tap, tap. The paint turned green! A green stripe went on the paper.

Red, yellow, blue. Three little pots. Blue and red made purple next. Leon looked at his rainbow. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. "I made it," said Leon. He held his painting up to the blue, blue sky.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story: Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a small red block first. It is light. He picks it up easy. Then he finds a big basket of blocks. He pulls and pulls. It will not move. It is heavy. His friend Mia comes over. She pats the basket. "Heavy and light are opposites," she says. They take the blocks out one by one. Each block is light. Carter stacks a big block at the bottom. He stacks a small block on the top. The tower grows tall. Mia brings a pillow, soft and light as a feather. She sets it on the top. The tower wiggles. It wiggles slow, then it falls fast. The pillow lands with a soft plop. Carter laughs. He stacks it again, slow and careful. "Look at the top," he says. The pillow sits there, all warm in the sun, while the cold juice cups wait on the shelf.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Mila wanted to find her red sock. It was lost somewhere in the playroom. She looked under the big teddy bear. Not there. She looked in the small toy box. Not there.

Then she saw her dog, Max, by the door. His tail was wagging fast. "Do you know where my sock is?" she asked. Max wagged his tail slow and happy. He was sitting on something. It was the red sock! But the sock was wet. Max had dripped water on it from his walk. "Wet sock," said Mila with a sigh. "I need a dry one."

Mila put the wet sock on the warm radiator. Mom helped her stay far from it, because it was hot. Then Mila found a dry blue sock in her drawer. She put it on her small foot. Max licked her toe, fast then slow. "Good boy," said Mila. "Now my foot is dry, and my sock is not!" She patted his soft ear, and they sat together on the rug.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Milan went to the park with his dad. He saw a red strawberry in the picnic basket. "Can I have it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. Milan loved strawberries.

First, Milan smelled the strawberry with his nose. It smelled sweet. Then he took a bite. It tasted big and sweet. Then he had a funny idea. What if he held his nose closed? He pinched his nose with his fingers. He took another bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like almost nothing. Milan opened his eyes wide. "Dad! My strawberry got quiet in my mouth!"

Dad laughed. "Try it again," he said. Milan let go of his nose. He took a bite. The sweet taste came back. He pinched his nose again. The taste got small again. "It comes and goes!" said Milan. He heard a dog bark with his ears. He touched the grass with his hands. "Dad, am I lucky to have all these parts?" asked Milan. Dad smiled and held up one more strawberry. "You try it too," said Milan.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She wanted to count her peas. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. What came after two? She could not remember. Her face began to look upset.

Mom slid the peas closer. "Sing your shoe song," Mom said. Aubrey knew that song. She sang it at school. She took a breath and tried.

"One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Oh! The word was hiding in the song. "Three, four, shut the door," she sang on. The peas heard her too. "Five, six, pick up sticks." She picked up her spoon like a stick. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." She laid her spoon down straight. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen," she sang, and giggled.

Dad peeked around his cup. "Sing it again," he said. Aubrey sang it again, slower. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Her little brother clapped his hands. He dropped a pea, and it rolled like a tiny green river across his plate.

"Three, four, shut the door," Aubrey sang. She shut the pea onto her spoon. "Five, six, pick up sticks." Mom gave her a carrot stick. Aubrey held it up high.

"Seven, eight, lay them straight," she sang. She laid the carrot next to the peas. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen." Dad made a hen face and said, "Cluck, cluck." Aubrey laughed so hard her spoon wobbled.

Then she ate the carrot, one big crunch. "Now you," she said to her brother. He opened his mouth wide. "One, two," she sang to him. He tried to sing too. "Oo," he said. Aubrey clapped for him. "Good job," she said. Then she took a bite of her peas.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Josephine wanted to build a big bed for her teddy. She found a big box at daycare. She pulled it. The box was too heavy. It did not move. "Oh no," said Josephine.

Her friend Sam ran over. He ran fast. Then he walked slow, so he would not bump her. Sam pulled too. Still the box did not move. It was heavy, heavy, heavy.

Miss Ruby came with a small white pillow. It was light. Josephine picked it up. Up, up, easy! She put the pillow in a small box. "A bed!" she said. She gave teddy a kiss. On the wall was a picture of a fire truck, big and red. Josephine yawned a big yawn. "Teddy is slow to sleep," she said. "Shh."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Paisley wanted a bedtime story about a funny rabbit. But Mama said, "Pick one book from your shelf." Paisley looked and looked. She found a book with a rabbit on the front.

She opened it near the end by mistake. "The rabbit is already asleep," she said. "The story is done!" Mama turned the book around. She went back to the front cover. She opened the first page. The rabbit woke up there and began to play.

"The story starts at the front," said Mama. Paisley tapped the cover. "Who made this up?" she asked. There were words on the front too. Mama put her finger under one name. "This is the author," she said. "She wrote the words."

Paisley traced the letters with her finger. Then she held the book up high. "I found the rabbit lady," she whispered. "Now read, Mama. Start at the front."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson was playing in the yard. He dug in the dirt with his little blue shovel. His hands got dirty. His knees got dirty too.

Then he heard a sound. "Lunch time!" Mom called from the door. Jaxson ran to the table. He saw bread, cheese, and apple slices. He reached for the bread with muddy hands.

Mom shook her head. "We wash our hands before we eat," she said. Jaxson looked at his dirty hands. One, two, ten muddy fingers. He ran to the sink. Mom turned on the water. It felt warm and bubbly. The soap smelled like flowers. The dirt went down, down, down. Now his hands were clean and shiny.

Jaxson ran back to the table. He picked up an apple slice. It tasted sweet and cool. Then he saw something funny. His little dog had muddy paws too. "Doggy needs the sink!" Jaxson said. Mom laughed. "Dogs get a bath outside, not in the sink." Jaxson giggled and took another big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brielle sat in her reading nook. She had a big card with letters on it. Mom pointed to a curvy letter. "This is S," Mom said. "It says sss." Brielle tried it. "Sss," she hissed like a little snake.

"Let's hunt for sss things," said Mom. Brielle looked around the nook. She found one sock under the cushion. "Sss sock!" she said. Sun came in the window and made a warm spot on the rug. "Sss sun!" she said. Then she saw her sand toy from the beach bag. "Sss sand!" Mom clapped. "Sun, sock and sand all start with S."

Brielle was mad when she could not find more. So she looked and looked. Then she found her stuffed snake. "Sss snake!" she giggled. Mom laughed too. "You found a surprise!" Brielle hugged the snake. "Sss, sss, sss," she whispered to it.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Paisley walks to the bookmobile with her mom. The big van is blue and white. It smells like paper and sunshine inside. Paisley wants a book about ponies. She wants one so, so much.

She finds a pony book on a low shelf. The cover feels rough. She hugs it tight. "This one," she says. "I want this one."

A man at the small desk smiles. "You can have your very own library card today," he says. He hands Paisley a little card. It is orange. Her name is on it. Paisley holds it with two hands.

Then the man scans the book. He scans her card too. "All done," he says. "Take the book home."

Paisley gasps. "Home? The book comes home with me?" She jumps up and down. "The card makes it mine for now. The card makes it mine!"

Mom laughs. "Yes. Your card means you can borrow it. We will read it tonight."

Paisley carries the book all the way. She holds it against her chest. It is a good feeling, warm like a hug.

At bedtime, Mom reads the pony book. Paisley pets the rough cover, soft and slow. "Good night, ponies," she says. "See you for three more stories tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Alice sits in her car seat. The seat belt clicks. Mom starts the car.

"Are we going to Mia's house now?" Alice says.

"Not now," Mom says. "We went to Mia's house yesterday. Today we are going to the store. Tomorrow we go to Mia's house again."

Alice looks out the window. A red truck goes by. Now it is here. Then it is gone.

"Today is now," Alice says.

"Yes," Mom says. "And tomorrow comes after today. First you sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Alice puts her hand on her mouth. She thinks about sleeping. She thinks about Mia's toys. Mia has a big heavy ball. They roll it on the floor.

At the store, Mom lifts a heavy bag of apples. Alice holds the bread. She is careful.

In the car again, the sun goes down. The sky turns pink, then gray.

"Sleep now," Alice says. "Mia tomorrow."

"Mia tomorrow," Mom says.

Alice yawns. She hugs her soft rabbit. The wheels hum on the road. The moon comes up, small and white.

"Hello, moon," Alice says. "See you after sleeping."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charles went to book club with his mama. There was a big rug and a basket of books. "A, B, C," said Miss Ana. "Letter B says buh. Letter D says duh."

Charles picked a book about a dog. But he read it his own way. "The bog says woof!" he said. He giggled and giggled.

"Is it a bog or a dog?" asked Miss Ana.

Charles looked. He counted the round parts. "One round part," he said. He turned his finger around and around. Then he saw it. "The b goes this way. The d goes that way."

Miss Ana laughed. "You did it, Charles."

Charles patted the picture. "It is a dog. A dog is an animal. A bog is not."

"Good thinking," said Miss Ana. "Now what is this word?"

It was "bed." Charles looked closely. Round parts, one this way, one that way. "Bed!" he said. "The dog can dry off on the bed. He is itchy and wet."

"That is a silly dog," laughed Miss Ana.

Charles turned the page. "D is for dog," he said. "Woof, woof!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone felt warm and dry in the sun. Mama set out a picnic on a red blanket. There were bread, apples, and cheese.

"We say a blessing before we eat," said Mama. "A blessing says thank you for the food."

Ivy did not know what to say. She looked at the bread. She looked at the apples. Her tummy felt empty and loud. She wanted to eat right now. But she waited, because Mama was waiting too.

Mama said the blessing. "Thank you for this food. Thank you for this day." Then she began the names. "One for Grandpa Ben. Two for Grandma Rose. Three for the farmer who grew the apples."

The farmer! Ivy had not thought about the farmer before. Someone had picked these apples. Someone had baked this bread. She picked up an apple and held it up high.

"I want to choose my own thank you," said Ivy. "Thank you to the sun for making the apples red. And thank you to Grandpa Ben for this picnic spot."

Mama's face grew a big smile. She clapped her hands, soft and slow. Then they ate the bread and cheese, and Ivy took one big bite of her apple.

"Sweet," said Ivy. "Grandpa Ben would like this spot."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Sofia held her red backpack tight. It was her first day of school. She walked down the big hallway with her mama. The floor was shiny. "I wonder how many doors there are," Sofia said. She counted one, two, three.

Then Sofia saw her friend Ben. Ben had been on the school bus that morning. "I stood up on the bus," Ben said. "I wanted to wave out the window at the sheep in the field." The sheep had white wool and stood by a red barn.

"What happened when you stood up?" Sofia asked. "The driver asked me to sit down," Ben said. "So I sat in my seat the whole way." Sofia nodded. "On the bus, we stay sitting in our seats," she said.

A teacher came to the door. "Time to mix the paint for our art table," she said. Sofia and Ben ran to the red table. Sofia picked up a brush. "I will paint the sheep by the barn," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Chloe went to the store with her dad. She held his hand in the parking lot. "Look at all the cars," she said. They were red, blue, yellow and green.

Chloe wanted a toy pig from the store. But first they had to cross the street. They stopped at the curb. The light was red. "The red car is stopping," said Chloe. Every car stood still. Then the light turned green. The cars rolled away. Dad gave her hand a little swing. "Green means the cars go," said Chloe. They waited for a new red light, and then no cars came, and they walked across.

Inside the store, Chloe found her pig. It was pink and heavy. She carried it in both arms. Dad smiled and opened the door for her. "Beep, beep," said Chloe, and rolled her pig down the walk like a little green car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was squished together. "Which row has more?" Mom asked. Oliver pointed at the long row. "That one! It goes way over there!"

Mom smiled. "Let's count them." Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the squished row. "One, two, three, four, five." He sat very still. Both rows had five!

Oliver pushed the long row together. He counted again. Still five! He spread the little row out wide. He counted one more time. "Five again!" He laughed out loud. A bee bumped against the window. Its buzz sounded excited too.

"Again!" said Oliver. Mom poured out ten soft marshmallows. Oliver spread them far apart. Then he pushed them into one pile. He counted both ways. Ten every time. "Mom! Look! Same!" Mom clapped her hands. Oliver counted the marshmallows one last time. "Ten!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jacob ran to the big playground. The sun felt hot on his nose. He wanted to ride down the slide. But a girl was banging a drum near the slide. Bang, bang, bang! It was so loud.

"The drum is loud," said Jacob. "My ears want quiet." The girl, Mia, stopped. She tapped the drum softly. Tap, tap. Now it was quiet. Jacob laughed. "Loud and quiet! The drum can do both?"

"Yes," said Mia. "Want to try?" Jacob tapped the drum. First loud, then quiet. His hands made it loud. His hands made it quiet. "I did it!" he said.

Then he rode down the slide, fast fast fast. He rolled to the small swing and went slow. On the way home, Dad gave Jacob a gift. It was a tiny drum, smelly like new shoes. Jacob tapped it. Just one little quiet tap. "Shh," he whispered. "The baby is napping."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Benjamin ran to the play corner. Mia was on the floor. She looked sad. Her doll had fallen down. It slid off the table and went bump.

"My doll is hurt," Mia said. She was scared to pick it up.

Teacher Ana knelt down. She picked up the doll. She turned it over slowly. "Look," she said. "The doll is fine. Toys cannot really feel. But we can pretend they do."

Mia gave the doll a hug. The doll felt all better. Benjamin watched with big eyes.

Then he picked up his bear. He made the bear jump off a block mountain. "Ouch!" he said in a bear voice. Then he gave the bear a hug. The bear smiled, because Benjamin made it smile.

"I will be the bear's dad," Benjamin said. "I will make him eat pretend soup."

He stirred the pot. He fed the bear one spoon. The bear ate it all up. Then the bear yawned a big yawn.

"Time for bed," Benjamin whispered. He laid the bear on a little blanket. He patted its back, soft, soft, soft. The bear closed its eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Claire was at Grandma's house. She wanted to make soup for Grandma. She found a small red pot in the toy box. She put in a wooden carrot and a felt pea. Then she found a shiny red berry on the rug. It was not real. It was a pretend berry, made of paper. Claire put the berry near her mouth.

Grandma shook her head fast. "Not in your mouth, sweet pea. That berry is just for pretending." Claire stopped. She looked at the paper berry. She held her pot up high instead.

"Now I will pretend to slurp my soup," said Claire. She tipped the pot to her lips. She made a big slurpy sound. Grandma laughed and clapped. Claire gave the wooden carrot a pretend taste too. "Mmm! It needs a song!" said Grandma. They sang together, and a bird began to fly past the window. It was the last bird of the morning, and it looked in at them. Claire waved her spoon at it. "Soup is ready!" she called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emily wanted her bedtime book about the bunny. She found it on her shelf. She opened the back cover by mistake. The pages went the wrong way.

"Try the front," said Dad. Emily turned the book around. She opened the front cover. Now the bunny came first. On the first page she saw small black marks. "What are those?" she asked.

"Those are words," said Dad. "They say the story." Dad read them out loud. The marks made the bunny story!

Emily loved the curly letters and the pictures. "Who drew the bunny?" she asked.

Dad pointed to a name on the first page. "This person drew the pictures. This person is the illustrator." The name was Kate.

Emily held the book up to the air. "Thank you, Kate!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Sarah ran to the library play corner. "Books!" she said. There was a big bin of things to sort.

Sarah dumped it out. A bear popped out. A shirt fell next. Then a sock. Then a banana toy and a hat.

Sarah made rows. The bear went with the toys. The banana went with the foods. She put the sock there too. Then she laughed. "No! Socks are not toys!"

She picked up the sock. It could bend and flop. The bear could not do that. The shirt could bend too. The hat could bend a little.

"Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes!" said Sarah. She put them in one pile. She patted the rough sock.

Then she found a picture book about a bear in a red hat. "Look, bear!" said Sarah. "He wears clothes too!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Joshua ran into the school cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family. Miss Ana put a warm loaf on the big table. It smelled wonderful.

Joshua grabbed the butter from the fridge. He tried to spread it. The butter was hard. It tore the bread into little holes. "Oh no," said Joshua. "The butter is too hard!"

Miss Ana set the butter dish on the counter. "We will wait a bit," she said. While they waited, Joshua counted. One spoon of honey. Two spoons of jam. He stirred the jam round and round. It swirled like red mud in a bowl.

Then Joshua touched the butter again. It was soft now! He spread it gently. One side. Two sides. Three sides. The bread looked perfect. Joshua jumped up and down. "I made family bread!" he said. He carried it to the door, holding it up high.
